issues: “Gumo [姑墨], also known as Jimo [亟黑]” → CBETA 舊謂姑黑，又曰亟黑: Guhei [姑黑], also Jihei [亟黑] (DM silently emends 黑 to 墨 in the first and misreads 亟黑 as Jimo; 姑墨 is the usual historical name, note as variant)
en_revised: From here, traveling westward for more than six hundred li, passing through a small desert, one arrives at the country of Bālukā (跋祿迦國) (formerly called Guhei [姑黑; elsewhere written 姑墨, Gumo], also called Jihei [亟黑]). The country of Bālukā measures more than six hundred li from east to west and more than three hundred li from south to north. The capital city of the country is five or six li in circumference. The soil, climate, human temperament, customs, and the rules of writing are the same as those of the country of Kuci (屈支國), though the language differs slightly. Fine felt and fine woolen cloth are highly valued by neighboring countries. There are several dozen saṃghārāmas (伽藍) with over one thousand monks, who study the teachings of the Small Vehicle (Hīnayāna) according to the Sarvāstivāda school (說一切有部).

issues: recurs from review_01: “traveling southeast” → 從此東南千餘里 has no 行 | “Feihan” → the note 㤄（敷發反） gives the reading fa: Fahan (Ferghana); DM ignores the reading-note
en_revised: Southeast from here, more than one thousand li, one reaches the country of Fahan (㤄捍國; Ferghana). The country of Fahan is over four thousand li in circuit, with mountains surrounding its four borders. The land is fertile, crops grow in abundance, flowers and fruits are plentiful, and it is suitable for raising sheep and horses. The climate is cold, the people are fierce and courageous by nature, their language differs from that of other countries, and their physical appearance is coarse and unattractive. For several decades, there has been no great ruler; the chieftains compete for power and refuse to submit to one another, relying on rivers and occupying strategic points to demarcate their territories and divide their capitals.

issues: “two hundred li from north to south” → 南北二百餘里: over two hundred
en_revised: To the east, one connects with the Onion Range (葱嶺) and arrives at the country of Kumēdha (拘謎陀國). The country of Kumēdha is over two thousand *li* from east to west and over two hundred *li* from north to south. It is situated in the midst of the Great Onion Range. The capital city of the country is over twenty *li* in circumference. To the southwest, it borders the Oxus River (縛芻河), and to the south, it connects with the country of Śikini (尸棄尼國). Crossing the Oxus River to the south, one reaches the country of Dharmasthiti (達摩悉鐵帝國), the country of Badakshān (鉢鐸創那國), the country of Yamgān (淫薄健國), the country of Kurān (屈浪拏國), the country of Himatala (呬摩呾羅國), the country of Pārghar (鉢利曷國), the country of Kishm (訖栗瑟摩國), the country of Rāgh (曷邏胡國), the country of Arni (阿利尼國), and the country of Mungān (瞢健國). From the country of Hu (活國), going southeast to the country of Khasta (闊悉多國) and the country of Andarāb (安呾羅縛國), the details are in the return record.

issues: recurs from review_01: “the country of Udyāna (銳秣陀國)” → 銳秣陀 is a different country (Ruimotuo, cf. 01.33; Beal Jui-mo-to), not Udyāna/Uḍḍiyāna (烏仗那) | “Seventy li” → 七十餘里 more than seventy | “Snow Mountains (Himālaya)” → 雪山 here the Hindu Kush; the gloss is DM’s addition | (the earlier “forty li” slip is fixed)
en_revised: More than fifty *li* to the northwest of the great city is the city of Trapuṣa (提謂城), and more than forty *li* to the north of that city is the city of Bhallika (波利城). In each of these cities there is a stūpa over three *zhang* in height. In the past, when the Tathāgata had first realized the fruit of Buddhahood, he arose from the Mahā-bodhi (菩提樹) and was on his way to the Deer Park. At that time, two merchants encountered his majestic radiance and, offering the provisions they carried for their journey, presented him with parched grain and honey. The World-Honored One explained to them the blessings of humans and gods, and they were the first to hear the five precepts and the ten virtues. Having heard his instruction, they requested something to worship, and the Tathāgata bestowed upon them his hair and nails. The two merchants, about to return to their own country, requested a ritual for paying homage. The Tathāgata took his *saṃghāṭī* (Original note: formerly called *saṃghīli*, which is incorrect), folded it square and placed it on the ground, then placed his *uttarāsaṅga* on top, followed by his *saṃkakṣikā* (Original note: formerly called *saṃghīci*, which is incorrect), then inverted his alms bowl, and stood his *khakkhara* staff upright; in this sequence, he formed a stūpa. The two men accepted his command and each returned to his own city, where they modeled their constructions after the holy design and built them accordingly; these were the very first stūpas in the Dharma of Śākyamuni. More than seventy *li* to the west of the city is a stūpa over two *zhang* high, which was built in the past during the time of Kāśyapa Buddha. From the great city, one goes southwest into the recesses of the Snow Mountains to reach the country of Ruimotuo (銳秣陀國).

issues: “Sphitavaras” → same city as 01.38.03, where DM writes “Śvetavatavāra” (霫蔽多伐剌祠); one form should be used
en_revised: More than thirty li to the south of the city of Śvetavatavāra (霫蔽多伐剌祠城), one arrives at Mount Aruṇa (阿路猱山). Its cliffs and ridges are steep and precipitous, and its rocky valleys are dark and deep. Every year, its peak increases in height by several hundred feet, and as soon as it appears to gaze toward Mount Śunāhila (䅳那呬羅山) in the country of Jāguḍa (漕矩吒國), it immediately collapses. I have heard from the local people: In the beginning, the deity Śunā (䅳那天神) came from afar, wishing to dwell on this mountain. The mountain deity was enraged and shook the ravines and valleys. The deity said, "Because you do not wish to accommodate me, you shake and move in this way. If you would show a little hospitality as a host to a guest, you would be filled with wealth and treasures. I am now going to Mount Śunāhila in the country of Jāguḍa; every year, when the time comes for me to receive the sacrifices and offerings of the king and his ministers, you should gaze toward me." Therefore, as soon as Mount Aruṇa has increased in height, it immediately collapses.

issues: “Piḍutuoqie (鞞鐸佉)” → hybrid of Sanskrit-like and pinyin; the original is uncertain (Julien vaitraka, Beal vidala, Watters piṇḍaka; Mizutani), transcribe Biduoqie
en_revised: To the southwest of the city is the mountain of Pīlusāra (比羅娑洛山; Tang language: "Elephant-Strong" [象堅]). The mountain deity takes the form of an elephant, hence it is called "Elephant-Strong." Formerly, when the Tathāgata was in the world, the Elephant-Strong deity invited the World-Honored One and twelve hundred great arhats. On the mountain peak there is a large flat rock; the Tathāgata sat upon it and accepted the deity's offerings. Afterward, King Aśoka (無憂王) built a stūpa on the flat rock, over one hundred feet high, which people today call the Elephant-Strong Stūpa. It is also said that it contains more than a sheng of the Tathāgata's relics. Below the mountain cliff to the north of the Elephant-Strong Stūpa is a nāga spring; this is where the Tathāgata, after receiving the deity's meal, and the arhats rinsed their mouths and chewed willow twigs, which then took root and became the dense grove that exists today. Later people established a saṃghārāma here, named Biduoqie (鞞鐸佉; Tang language: "Chewing Willow Twigs"). Traveling east from here for over six hundred li, through continuous mountains and valleys with steep peaks and precipitous cliffs, one crosses the Black Range (黑嶺), enters the territory of North India, and reaches the country of Lampā (濫波國) (Original note: territory of North India).

issues: “eight hundred li” → 南北八百餘里 over eight hundred | “formerly called Gandhavatī” → 乾陀衛 is an old Chinese transcription (Qiantuowei), not a Sanskrit form | “rock honey” → 石蜜 rock sugar | “one hundred deva temples” → 天祠百數 deva temples numbering about a hundred / some hundreds
en_revised: From here, traveling southeast through mountain valleys for over five hundred li, one reaches the country of Gandhāra (健馱邏國) (formerly called Qiantuowei [乾陀衛], which is incorrect; it is in the region of North India). The country of Gandhāra is over one thousand li from east to west and over eight hundred li from north to south. To the east, it borders the Sindhu (信度河) River. The great capital city of the country is called Puruṣapura (布路沙布邏), which is over forty li in circumference. The royal lineage has died out, and it is subject to the country of Kāpiśī (迦畢試國). The towns and villages are desolate, and the inhabitants are few; in one corner of the palace city, there are over a thousand households. The crops are abundant, flowers and fruits are lush, there is much sugarcane, and it produces rock sugar. The climate is warm and hot, with almost no frost or snow. The people are timid and cowardly; they are fond of studying the arts and classics, and they mostly revere heterodox paths, having little faith in the True Dharma. Since ancient times, this has been the birthplace of various masters in the Indian region who composed treatises, such as Nārāyaṇa-deva, Asanga Bodhisattva, Vasubandhu Bodhisattva, Dharmatrāta, Manoratha, and the Venerable Pārśva. There are over one thousand saṃghārāmas, which are ruined, desolate, and overgrown with weeds; many of the stūpas are dilapidated. There are about a hundred deva temples, where heterodox practitioners live together.

issues: partly recurs from review_02-03: “followed a boar and lost his way; he offered a reward of one hundred million gold coins to anyone who could find his tracks” → 逐豕失蹤，有尋知迹者，賞一億金錢: he lost the boar’s track, someone found the trail, and [the king] rewarded him with 100 million — an actual payment, which Manoratha then matched for a haircut, hence the king’s shame (Mizutani: 見つけ出したものがあったので…とらせた) | fixed since the earlier review: Manoratha (not the king) paid the barber; the non-Buddhists “who had debated with” Manoratha
en_revised: To the west of the great stūpa is an old monastery, which was built by King Kaniṣka (迦膩色迦王). With its multi-storied pavilions and tiered terraces, its layered platforms and open windows, it was designed to summon high-ranking monks and to manifest auspicious blessings. Although it has fallen into ruin, it is still considered a work of marvelous craftsmanship. The number of monks has dwindled, and they all study the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna). Since the monastery was built, extraordinary people have appeared there from time to time. The pure influence of the various masters who composed treatises and attained the holy fruits still lingers, and their supreme virtues have not been extinguished. On the third story of the pavilion is the room of the Venerable Pārśva (波栗濕縛; in Tang language, "Ribs" [脇]), which has long since collapsed, though a commemorative marker still stands. Originally, when the Venerable was a teacher of the Brahmins, he was nearly eighty years old when he left his home and donned the dyed robes. The youths in the city mocked him, saying: "What a foolish, decrepit old man, how shallow his wisdom! Those who leave home have two tasks: first, to practice meditation; second, to recite the scriptures. Now, in your senility, you have made no progress; you merely clutter the ranks of the pure, knowing only how to fill your belly." When the Venerable Pārśva heard these reproaches, he took leave of the people of the time and made a vow, saying: "If I do not master the principles of the Tripiṭaka, sever the desires of the three realms, attain the six supernatural powers, and possess the eight liberations, I shall never let my ribs touch a mat!" From then on, he felt only that the days were insufficient; whether walking, sitting, or standing in contemplation, he studied the doctrines by day and practiced quiet meditation with a concentrated mind by night. After three years, he had mastered the Tripiṭaka, severed the desires of the three realms, and attained the three types of clear wisdom. The people of the time respected him and thus called him the Venerable Pārśva (the Venerable Ribs). To the east of the room of the Venerable Pārśva is an old chamber where the Bodhisattva Vasubandhu (世親) composed the *Abhidharmakośa-śāstra* (阿毘達磨俱舍論); out of respect, people have sealed it and marked it with a memorial. About fifty paces south of Vasubandhu’s room is a second-story pavilion where the Master Manoratha (末笯曷剌他; translated into Chinese as Ruyi, "As-Desired") composed the *Vibhāṣā-śāstra* (毘婆沙論). This master appeared one thousand years after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa. In his youth, he was fond of learning and possessed talent and eloquence; his reputation spread far and wide, and both the clergy and the laity turned their hearts toward him. At that time, King Vikramāditya (毘訖羅摩阿迭多; translated into Chinese as Chaori, "Surpassing the Sun") of the country of Śrāvastī (室羅伐悉底國) extended his majestic influence to distant lands and brought all of India under his rule; every day he distributed five hundred million gold coins to provide for the poor, the destitute, the orphaned, and the solitary. The treasurer, fearing that the national resources would be exhausted, offered a remonstrance, saying: "Your Majesty’s awe-inspiring power reaches foreign peoples and your benevolence extends even to insects; I pray you increase the distribution by another five hundred million gold coins to relieve the needy of the four quarters. Once the treasury is empty, we shall have to levy further taxes on the landholders; when heavy taxation continues without end and the cries of resentment spread everywhere, then the sovereign above will enjoy the reputation of being a generous provider, while the ministers below will bear the blame for being disrespectful." The King replied, "To gather the surplus and provide for the insufficient is not for the sake of my own luxury or the waste of national resources." He then added five hundred million coins to benefit the poor and needy. Later, while hunting, he pursued a boar and lost its track; someone found the trail, and he rewarded him with one hundred million gold coins. Master Manoratha once had someone shave his head, and he immediately bestowed one hundred million gold coins upon him; the state historian of that country recorded this accordingly. The king was ashamed to be surpassed and felt constant resentment, desiring to publicly humiliate the Master of Shastras, Manoratha (如意論師). He summoned one hundred practitioners of heterodox schools who were of high virtue and profound learning, and issued an order, saying: "Wishing to focus my attention and wander through the various true realms, I find the heterodox paths to be chaotic and my mind at a loss as to where to turn. Now, I shall examine their relative merits so that I may focus my devotion." When they gathered for the debate, he issued a further order, saying: "The heterodox masters are all outstanding men. The assembly of Śramaṇa (沙門) practitioners should be well-versed in their own doctrines; if they win, I shall honor the Buddha-Dharma, but if they lose, I shall execute the monks." Thereupon, Manoratha questioned the various heterodox teachers, and ninety-nine of them had already retreated in defeat. Only one remained in the lower seat, whom he regarded with contempt. They then engaged in a vigorous debate, which touched upon the subject of smoke and fire. The king and the heterodox teacher both shouted out: "Master Manoratha’s words and reasoning are flawed! It is a common principle of reality that smoke comes first and fire follows." Although Manoratha wished to explain the difficulty, no one would listen. Ashamed at being publicly humiliated, he bit off his tongue and wrote a warning to his disciple, Vasubandhu (世親), saying: "Do not contend for the great truth among a crowd of partisans; do not debate correct doctrine among the deluded masses." Having finished speaking, he died. Not long after, the king, Vikramāditya (超日王), lost his kingdom, and a rising king took up the mandate, showing respect for the wise and virtuous. The Bodhisattva Vasubandhu, wishing to wipe away the previous shame, came and said to the king: "Great King, you rule with holy virtue and are the master and life-force of all sentient beings." "My late teacher Manoratha (如意) had exhausted the study of the most profound mysteries, yet the former king, harboring an old grudge, allowed the masses to humiliate his great reputation; having received his guidance and instruction, I wish to redress the grievance done to my predecessor." The king, knowing that Manoratha was a man of wisdom and admiring the noble character of Vasubandhu (世親), summoned the various non-Buddhists who had debated with Manoratha. Vasubandhu restated the principles of his predecessor, and the non-Buddhists admitted defeat and withdrew.

issues: interlinear notes left untranslated: “(唐言世友; …)” → (in the Tang language, Shiyou, “World-Friend”; …); “(唐言法救; …)” → (in the Tang language, Fajiu, “Dharma-Saviour”; …)
en_revised: Traveling northeast from the monastery of King Kaniṣka for more than fifty *li*, one crosses a great river and arrives at the city of Puṣkalāvatī (布色羯邏伐底城). It is fourteen or fifteen *li* in circumference. The inhabitants are prosperous, and the houses are connected throughout. Outside the west gate of the city is a temple to a deva; the image of the deva is majestic, and miraculous manifestations occur there in succession. To the east of the city is a stūpa built by King Aśoka, which is the place where the four past Buddhas preached the Dharma. In ancient times, many sages and worthies from Central India descended here to guide living beings. It was here that the śāstra-master Vasumitra (in the Tang language, Shiyou [世友], “World-Friend”; the old name, Hexumiduo [和須蜜多], is incorrect) composed the *Abhidharma-prakaraṇa-pāda-śāstra* (眾事分阿毘達磨論). Four or five *li* to the north of the city is an old monastery; its courtyards and buildings are desolate, and the number of monks is small, yet they all follow and study the teachings of the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna). It was here that the śāstra-master Dharmatrāta (in the Tang language, Fajiu [法救], “Dharma-Saviour”; the old name, Damoduoluo [達磨多羅], is incorrect) composed the *Saṃyuktābhidharma-hṛdaya-śāstra* (雜阿毘達磨論). Beside the monastery is a stūpa several hundred feet high, built by King Aśoka. Its carved wood and patterned stones are quite unlike the work of human hands. This is where the Buddha Śākyamuni, in a former life when he was a king practicing the bodhisattva path, followed the desires of living beings and gave alms without fatigue, regarding the loss of his own body as if it were nothing; in this land, he was king for a thousand lives, and in this very place, he gave up his eyes for a thousand lives. Not far to the east of the place where he gave up his eyes are two stone stūpas, each over one hundred feet high. The one on the right was erected by the Brahmā King (梵王), and the one on the left was built by the Lord of Devas (天帝); they were adorned with exquisite and precious jewels. After the Tathāgata entered nirvāṇa, the jewels transformed into stone; although the foundations have collapsed and sunk, they are still considered lofty.

issues: recurs from review_02-03: “giving his father the king’s great elephant to a Brahmin” → 以父王大象施婆羅門: giving the great elephant of his father the king to a Brahmin (DM wording reads as if given to the father)
en_revised: To the north of the city is a stūpa, which is where Prince Sudāna (translated into Chinese as "Good Tooth") was rebuked and banished for giving the great elephant of his father, the king, to a Brahmin; he looked back to thank his countrymen and, having passed through the city gates, bade them farewell here. Beside it is a monastery with more than fifty monks, all of whom are students of the Hīnayāna. In the past, the master Īśvara (translated into Chinese as "Self-Existent") composed the *Abhidharmadīpa-śāstra* here.

issues: recurs: “converted the later followers of the sage Pāṇini” → 化波爾尼仙後進: converted a later follower of Pāṇini (the boy of the story) | recurs: “Five hundred years after” → 垂五百年 nearly five hundred years | recurs: stray closing quotation mark after the bats sentence (the Arhat’s speech continues to “beyond description”) | “The children of this town, as later followers, look up to his virtue” → 此邑之子，後進仰德: he was a son of this town; later generations revere his virtue | the final note （唐言苑…北印度境） is broken: DM closes the bracket after “Cakravartin king” and puts the rest of the note into the main text | “Udakhāṇḍa” / “Udakahāṇḍa” inconsistent
en_revised: Traveling over twenty li northwest from the city of Udakhāṇḍa (烏鐸迦漢荼城), one reaches the town of Śalātura (婆羅覩邏邑), which is the birthplace of the ṛṣi Pāṇini (波爾尼仙), the author of the Śabdavidyā-śāstra (聲明論). At the beginning of remote antiquity, written characters were numerous and extensive, but as time passed through the kalpa of destruction, the world became a void, until the long-lived deities descended to inspire both the sacred and the secular, and from this, literary records were born. Since that time, their sources have proliferated. King Brahmā and Lord Indra created models according to the needs of the times, and the various immortals of heterodox paths each devised their own scripts; people followed their predecessors and vied to practice what was handed down, but students' efforts were in vain, as it was difficult to investigate the systems in detail. When the human lifespan was one hundred years, there was the ṛṣi Pāṇini, who was born with great wisdom and broad learning. Pitying the decadence of the age, he wished to prune away the superficial and false, and to edit and refine the cumbersome and redundant. He traveled to various regions to inquire after the Way, and upon meeting Maheśvara (自在天), he expressed his intention to compose a work. Maheśvara said, "Excellent! I shall assist you." Having received these instructions, the ṛṣi withdrew and applied his mind to deep reflection, collecting a vast array of words to compose a lexicon consisting of one thousand stanzas, each containing thirty-two syllables. It exhausted the depths of both the present and the past, and summarized the entirety of literary language. He sealed it and presented it to the king, who found it most extraordinary and issued a decree throughout the kingdom to make it universally studied, rewarding anyone who could recite it with mastery with one thousand gold coins. This is why the tradition of teacher and student has been passed down and flourished in the present age. Consequently, the Brahmins in this town are men of great learning and high talent, possessing broad knowledge and excellent memories. In the town of Śalātura (婆羅覩邏邑) there is a stūpa, which is the place where an Arhat converted a later follower of the sage Pāṇini. Nearly five hundred years after the Tathāgata had passed away, a great Arhat traveling from the country of Kaśmīra (迦濕彌羅國) arrived here and saw a Brahmin beating and scolding a young boy. The Arhat asked the Brahmin, "Why are you tormenting this child?" The Brahmin replied, "I am making him study the *Śabdavidyā-śāstra* (聲明論), but his progress is not timely." The Arhat smiled gently. The old Brahmin said, "The nature of a Śramaṇa is compassion and pity for all living beings. I wish to hear the reason for your laughter." The Arhat said, "It is not easy to speak of this, for I fear it will cause deep doubt. Have you ever heard that the sage Pāṇini composed the *Śabdavidyā-śāstra* and left it as a teaching for the world?" The Brahmin replied, "He was a son of this town; later generations look up to his virtue, and his image is still here." The Arhat said, "This child of yours is that very sage. Because he possessed a powerful memory, he indulged in the study of worldly texts, discussing only heterodox doctrines without investigating the true principles. His spiritual wisdom was wasted in vain, and his transmigration has not yet ceased; it is only by riding on the merit of his remaining good deeds that he has become your beloved son. However, the literary expressions of worldly texts merely exhaust one's efforts; how can they compare to the holy teachings of the Tathāgata, which nourish merit and wisdom in the dark? Formerly, on the shore of the Southern Sea, there was a withered tree where five hundred bats lived in holes. Some merchants stopped under this tree. At that time, it was windy and cold, and everyone was hungry and freezing. They gathered firewood and brush, and kindled a fire beneath it. The smoke and flames gradually intensified, and the withered tree caught fire. Among the merchants, there was one trader who, after the middle of the night, was reciting the Abhidharma-piṭaka (阿毘達磨藏). Although those bats were distressed by the fire, they loved the sound of the Dharma and endured it without leaving, and thus they met their end there. Following their karma, they were reborn, all obtaining human bodies. They left their homes to study and practice, and by virtue of having heard the sound of the Dharma, they were intelligent and wise, all attaining the holy fruit and becoming fields of merit for the world. Recently, King Kaniṣka (迦膩色迦王) and the Venerable Pārśva (脇尊者) summoned five hundred sages in the country of Kaśmīra (迦濕彌羅國) to compose the Vibhāṣā-śāstra (毘婆沙論); these are the very same five hundred bats from the withered tree. Although I am unworthy, I am one of that number. This shows that the superior and the inferior are truly different, and the flying and the crawling are vastly distinct. You should now allow your beloved son to leave home; the merit of leaving home is beyond description." When the Arhat had spoken these words, he displayed his supernatural powers and suddenly vanished. The brahmin was deeply filled with reverence and wonder, and after praising the goodness of this for a long time, he told his neighbors everything. He then allowed his son to leave home to study and practice, and consequently turned to the faith, honoring the Triple Gem. The villagers followed his transformation, and their devotion remains intense to this day. Traveling north from the city of Udakhāṇḍa (烏鐸迦漢荼城), crossing mountains and wading through rivers for more than six hundred li, one arrives at the country of Uḍḍiyāna (烏仗那國) (Original note: In the language of the Tang, this means "garden," as it was formerly the pleasure garden of a Cakravartin king. It was formerly called Wuchang (烏場) or sometimes Wucha (烏茶), but both are incorrect. It is within the territory of North India).

issues: “The valley stream branches to the west, but as one ascends eastward against the current” → 谷水西派，逆流東上: the valley stream branches westward and flows back up to the east (the stream itself, a marvel; not the traveller) | variant as before: CBETA 方石如塔, Mizutani 榻
en_revised: More than four hundred *li* to the south of the city of Maṅgala (瞢揭釐城), one reaches Mount Hiḍḍa (醯羅山). The valley stream branches to the west and flows back up eastward against its course; various flowers and strange fruits cover the gullies and line the cliffs. The peaks and crags are perilous, and the streams and valleys wind and meander; sometimes one hears the sound of loud talking, and sometimes one hears the strains of music. Square stones resemble pagodas, appearing as if fashioned by craftsmen, stretching out in succession and spreading through the cliffs and valleys. This is where the Tathāgata in a former life sacrificed his body and life to hear half a stanza (Original note: Formerly it was called *jie* (伽), which is an abbreviation of the Sanskrit. Some call it *jieta* (偈他), which is a corruption of the Sanskrit sound. Following the correct pronunciation now, it should be called *gāthā* (伽他). *Gāthā* means *song* (頌) in the language of Tang, a *song* being thirty-two syllables) of the Dharma.

issues: “a great mountain (Pravaragiri)” → 大山側: no name in the Chinese (same addition flagged for 03.06.08 in the earlier review) | notes half-translated (“唐言大林 - …”); render as notes | variant as before: 薩縛達之王 / 薩縛達多王
en_revised: More than two hundred li south of the city of Maṅgala (瞢揭釐城), by the side of a great mountain, one reaches the Mahāvana (摩訶伐那; in the language of Tang, "Great Forest" [大林]) Monastery. This is where the Tathāgata, in a former life when practicing the bodhisattva path as a king named Sarvadatta (薩縛達; in the language of Tang, "All-Bestowing" [一切施]), having fled his enemies and abandoned his kingdom, traveled in secret to this place and encountered a poor brahmin who had come to beg for alms. Having already lost his royal position and having nothing to give, he ordered the brahmin to bind him and take him captive to the enemy king, hoping that the reward money could be used as a gift of charity in return.

issues: interlinear note 摩愉（摩言豆, read 唐言豆） omitted: “in the Tang language, ‘Bean’” | “(Mayuṇḍa)” → invented form, not in the text (Mizutani: Watters’ mayūkha rejected; Julien masūra)
en_revised: Thirty or forty li to the northwest of the Mahāvana (Great Forest) Monastery, descending the mountain, one reaches the Mayū (摩愉; in the Tang language, "Bean") Monastery. There is a stūpa over one hundred feet high. On a large square stone at its side are the footprints of the Tathāgata, left when the Buddha formerly stepped upon this stone and emitted a koṭi of rays of light to illuminate the Mahāvana Monastery, while preaching Jātaka stories for the sake of all humans and devas. Below the base of this stūpa is a stone, yellowish-white in color, which is always moist and oily. It is here that the Tathāgata, in the past while practicing the bodhisattva path, split his bones to write down the scriptures in order to hear the true Dharma.

issues: recurs (punctuation): “medical treatments were ineffective, and deaths followed one after another” → read 醫療無功，道死相屬: the dead lay one after another on the roads (CBETA punctuates 無功道，死相屬; Mizutani, Beal take 道死) | fixed since the earlier review: 代鴿 now “the place where the dove was ransomed”
en_revised: Traveling more than two hundred *li* northwest from the place where the dove was ransomed, one enters the Sanirāja River valley and reaches the Sarpauṣadhi (which means "Snake Medicine" in the language of Tang) Monastery. There is a *stūpa* here, more than eighty feet high. It is said that in the past, when the Tathāgata was Indra, a time of famine and pestilence occurred; medical treatments were ineffective, and the dead lay one after another on the roads. Indra, moved by compassion and wishing to provide relief, transformed his body into that of a giant python, lying dead in the valley, and proclaimed it to all from the air. Those who heard were moved and rejoiced, rushing to the site; as they cut pieces from the body, it would immediately regenerate, curing their hunger and their illnesses. Not far to the side is a large *stūpa* of Soma. It is said that in the past, when the Tathāgata was Indra, during a time of pestilence, he took pity on all sentient beings and transformed his body into a Soma snake; all who consumed it were restored to health and comfort. Beside the stone cliff to the north of the Sanirāja River, there is a *stūpa*. Sick people who come here to pray are often cured of their ailments. In the past, when the Tathāgata was a peacock king, he came to this place with his flock; driven by heat and thirst, they sought water but could not find any, so the peacock king pecked the cliff with his beak, causing a spring to gush forth. This has now become a pool, and drinking from or bathing in it cures illnesses. The tracks of the peacock are still visible on the stone.

issues: “vihāra (mūla-gandha-kuṭī)” → 精舍: the gloss is DM’s addition
en_revised: Crossing the great river thirty or forty li to the west of the stone stūpa, one arrives at a vihāra (精舍) containing an image of the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara (in Tang language, Guanzizai. When the characters are combined and the sounds are linked, the Sanskrit is as above; when the text is separated and the sounds are analyzed, "Avalokita" is translated as "Guan" [Observing], and "Īśvara" is translated as "Zizai" [Sovereign]. Former translations such as Guangshiyin, or Guanshiyin, or Guanshizizai, are all erroneous). His majestic spiritual influence is secretly bestowed, his miraculous traces are clearly manifest, and both the ordained and the laity flock there, offering worship without interruption.

issues: recurs: “wandering aimlessly” → 虛遊: travelling through the air (on the goose) | recurs: “As for the matter of intimate relations, I have not heard of such an intention” → 命有讌私，未聞來旨: though fate has brought us to intimacy, I have not yet heard [my parents’] will | recurs: “to execute those who do not submit” → 以誅後伏: those slow to submit | recurs: “the kings finally granted him an equal share” → 遂先均授: divided equally, giving him his share first | “嗢嗾羅犀那” → the text has 嗢呾羅犀那 (wrong character in DM) | “the people of this country often suffer” → 國族: the ruling clan of this country | ambiguous, DM kept (as before): 謝曰此言非冀; 宗親擯逐
en_revised: One hundred and fifty li northwest of the statue of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, one arrives at the mountain of Lamboura (藍勃盧山). On the mountain ridge is a dragon lake, over thirty li in circumference; its green waves are vast and expansive, and its clear waters are as bright as a mirror. In the past, when King Virūḍhaka (毘盧釋迦王) attacked the Śākyas, four men resisted the army; they were expelled by their kinsmen and each fled in a different direction. One of these Śākyas, having left the capital, was exhausted from his travels and stopped midway. At that time, a wild goose flew before him; since it was tame and friendly, he mounted it. The goose flew and landed beside this lake. The Śākya, having traveled through the air far to a foreign land, was lost and did not know the way, so he took a nap in the shade of a tree. The young daughter of the dragon of the lake was wandering along the water's edge when she suddenly saw the Śākya; fearing her appearance was inappropriate, she transformed into human form and approached to stroke him. The Śākya was startled awake and asked, "I am a weary traveler, why do you show me such intimacy?" He then pressed her with great earnestness, forcing himself upon her in the wilderness. The woman said, "I have my parents' instructions, which I respect and do not violate. Although I am honored by your attention, I have not received their command." The Śākya asked, "The mountain valleys are dark and remote; where is your home?" She replied, "I am the dragon daughter of this lake. I respectfully heard that your noble clan was wandering in exile, and as I happened to be out for a stroll, I dared to offer comfort for your fatigue. Though fate has brought us to intimacy, I have not yet heard my parents’ will. Furthermore, due to accumulated karma, I have received this dragon body; humans and animals follow different paths, and such a thing is unheard of." The Śākya said, "If you grant me this one word, my long-held desire will be fulfilled." The dragon girl said, "I respectfully hear your command; I submit to whatever you decide." The Śākya then made a vow in his heart: "By whatever power of merit I possess, let this dragon girl's entire body be transformed into that of a human." Moved by the power of his merit, the dragon then changed her form; having attained a human body, she was deeply overjoyed. She thanked the Śākya, saying, "Due to my accumulated evil karma, I have been wandering in the lower realms. Fortunately, I have received your kind attention, and through the application of your merit, this wretched body held for vast kalpas has been transformed in an instant. I wish to repay this virtue, but even shattering my body would not be enough. I desire to accompany you, but I am constrained by the opinions of others. I wish to inform my parents, and then prepare the rites." The dragon girl returned to the pool and told her parents, "Today while out on an excursion, I suddenly met a member of the Śākya clan; moved by the power of his merit, I have been transformed into a human. My heart is set on a happy union, and I venture to state the facts." The Dragon King, pleased with the human realm and holding the holy clan in high regard, acceded to his daughter's request. He then emerged from the pool and thanked the Śākya, saying, "You have not shunned those of a different species, but have lowered your noble status to accommodate the lowly. I wish for you to visit my dwelling, where I dare to offer you my service." The Śākya accepted the Dragon King's invitation and went to his residence. There, within the dragon palace, they prepared the rites for a personal wedding, and in the joy of their new union, they indulged in the utmost pleasure. However, the Śākya, seeing the dragon's form, felt constant fear and disgust, and wished to take his leave. The Dragon King stopped him, saying, "I hope you will not go far away, but reside in this neighborhood. I shall cause you to occupy territory, bear a great title, command subjects, and enjoy a long-lasting dynasty." The Śākya declined, saying, "This is not what I desire." The Dragon King placed a precious sword into a chest and covered it with a fine white cotton cloth. He said to the Śākya, "I hope you will take this cloth and present it to the king. The king will surely receive this tribute from a man from afar in person, and at that moment, you can slay him. By then seizing his kingdom, would that not be excellent?" The Śākya accepted the dragon’s instructions and went to present it. As the King of Udyāna (烏仗那) personally lifted the cloth, the Śākya seized his sleeve and stabbed him. The attendants and guards were in an uproar on the palace steps, but the Śākya brandished his sword and declared, "The sword I wield was bestowed upon me by the divine dragon to execute those who are slow to submit and to behead those who are not loyal." All were awed by his divine martial prowess and elevated him to the high throne. Thereupon, he reformed the corrupt administration, honored the virtuous, and relieved the suffering. Having done this, he mobilized a great assembly and prepared a royal procession to go to the dragon palace to report his success and bring the dragon girl back to the capital. Because the dragon girl’s past karma was not yet exhausted and residual retribution remained, whenever they were in private, nine dragon heads would emerge from her head. The Śākya, fearful and disgusted, did not know what plan to devise, but when he caught her sleeping, he cut them off with a sharp blade. The dragon girl, startled from her sleep, said, "This is not to the benefit of our descendants; not only is my life somewhat injured, but your offspring shall suffer from headaches." Therefore, the royal clan of this country often suffers from this affliction; although it is not continuous, it flares up from time to time. After the Śākya passed away, his son succeeded to the throne; this was King Uttarasena (嗢呾羅犀那; Tang dynasty translation: "Superior Army"). After King Uttarasena succeeded to the throne, his mother lost her sight. The Tathāgata, having subdued the dragon Apalāla (阿波邏羅), was returning and descended through the air into the palace. King Uttarasena happened to be out hunting, so the Tathāgata briefly explained the essentials of the Dharma to his mother. Having encountered the Holy One and heard the Dharma, she immediately regained her sight. The Tathāgata asked, "Your son is of my clan; where is he now?" The mother replied, "He went out hunting this morning and is now on his way back." The Tathāgata and the great assembly were about to depart. The King’s mother said, "It is only by my good fortune that I gave birth into this holy clan; the Tathāgata has shown great compassion by personally visiting us. My son is just now returning, so I pray you stay and wait a moment." The World-Honored One said, "This man is of my clan. He can be awakened to faith by hearing the teachings; he does not require personal instruction to arouse his resolve. I shall depart. When he returns, tell him: 'The Tathāgata is going from here to the city of Kuśinagara (拘尸城) to enter nirvāṇa among the śāla trees; you should obtain the relics and make offerings to them yourself.'" The Tathāgata and the great assembly then rose into the void and departed. King Uttarasena was out hunting and saw from afar a brilliant light shining in the palace; suspecting a fire, he stopped his hunt and returned. He then saw that his mother had regained her sight, and he asked joyfully, "How long was I gone that such an auspicious response occurred, restoring my mother's vision as it was before?" The mother replied, "After you went out, the Tathāgata arrived here; upon hearing the Buddha preach the Dharma, I regained my sight." "The Tathāgata has gone from here to the śāla trees in the city of Kuśinagara (拘尸城) to enter nirvana; he summons you to come quickly to receive a portion of his relics." When the king heard this, he wailed with grief and collapsed to the ground. After a long time, he regained his senses and ordered his carriage to hasten to the site. By the time he arrived between the twin trees, the Buddha had already entered nirvana. At that time, the various kings looked down upon his borderland status and, treasuring the relics, did not wish to share them with him. Then, the assembly of devas and humans restated the Buddha’s intention; having heard this, the kings divided the relics equally, giving him his share first.

issues: “formerly called Duoshita, and also Doushuta” → 兜率他 Doushuaita, 兜術他 Doushuta
en_revised: Going northeast from the city of Maṅgala (瞢揭釐城), crossing mountains and traversing valleys, and heading upstream along the Indus River (信度河), the path is perilous and the valleys are dark and gloomy. One must tread on rope bridges or cling to iron chains; plank paths are suspended over voids, bridges are built precariously high, and one must step on wooden pegs driven into the rock. After traveling over a thousand *li*, one reaches the valley of Darada (達麗羅川), which is the old capital of the kingdom of Udyāna (烏仗那國). It produces much gold and saffron. Beside a great monastery in the Darada valley, there is a carved wooden statue of the Bodhisattva Maitreya (慈氏菩薩). Its golden color shines brightly, and its spiritual efficacy is subtly pervasive. It is over a hundred feet tall and was created by the Arhat Madhyāntika (末田底迦) (Original note: formerly called Madhyandina, which is an incorrect abbreviation). The Arhat used his supernatural powers to transport a craftsman up to the Tuṣita Heaven (覩史多天) (Original note: formerly called Doushuaita [兜率他], and also Doushuta [兜術他], which are incorrect) to personally observe the Bodhisattva's exquisite features. After three such visits, the work was finally completed. Ever since this statue came into existence, the Dharma has flowed toward the eastern regions.

issues: recurs: “The king, hearing this” → 王或聞說: 或 = 惑, the king, deluded, heard her (Mizutani: 惑いをもって) | recurs: “we have not yet been able to act upon it” → 尚未可依: it should not yet be obeyed (Mizutani: なお信用はできません) | recurs: “Mahā-bodhi (菩提樹) monastery” → 菩提樹伽藍: the Bodhi-tree monastery | recurs: “The day after tomorrow” → 吾於後日: on a later day, soon | “Snow Mountains (Himālaya)” → gloss is DM’s addition | ambiguous, DM kept (as before): 諸豪世俗
en_revised: To the southeast of the city, on the northern side of the South Hill, there is a stūpa over a hundred feet high, built by King Aśoka (無憂王) at the place where his son, Prince Kuṇāla (拘浪拏), had his eyes gouged out after being falsely accused by his stepmother. Blind people who pray here often have their sight restored. This prince was the son of the first queen; he was elegant in appearance and had long been renowned for his kindness and benevolence. After the first queen passed away, the stepmother, who was arrogant and lewd, gave free rein to her muddled stupidity and privately attempted to seduce the prince. The prince wept, took the blame upon himself, and withdrew to apologize for his perceived offense. Seeing her advances rejected, the stepmother’s fury intensified. Waiting for a moment when the king was at leisure, she said composedly, "Takṣaśilā (呾叉始羅) is a strategic key to the kingdom; can it be entrusted to anyone other than a close royal scion? Now, the prince is known for his benevolence and filial piety, and because he is both a relative and a man of virtue, public opinion favors him." The king, deluded, heard her and was pleased by the treacherous scheme; he immediately summoned the prince and admonished him, saying, "I have inherited the legacy of my ancestors to continue their rule, and I live in constant fear of losing it and thereby bringing shame upon the late kings. Takṣaśilā is the throat and belt of the kingdom, and I now appoint you to govern that country. The affairs of the state are heavy and complex, and the sentiments of the people are devious and mixed; do not act rashly or carelessly, lest you damage the foundation of our inheritance. Whenever there is a summons, verify it with my tooth-seal. The seal is in my mouth; how could there be any error?" Thereupon, the prince accepted the command and came to govern. As time passed, the stepmother’s anger grew; she forged a royal decree, sealed it with purple clay, and while the king was sleeping, she stole his teeth to make the impression, then dispatched a messenger to deliver the letter of condemnation. The assisting ministers knelt to read it, looking at one another in dismay. The prince asked, "Why are you so sorrowful?" They replied, "The Great King has issued a command, a written decree reprimanding the prince, ordering that your two eyes be gouged out and that you be exiled and abandoned in the mountain valleys, leaving you and your wife to live or die as fate decides. Although this command exists, it should not yet be obeyed. We should now request a confirmation, and you should present yourself bound to await your punishment." The prince said, "If a father grants death to his son, how can it be refused? The tooth-seal serves as the signet; truly, there can be no error." He ordered a Caṇḍāla to gouge out his eyes. Once his eyes were blinded, he begged for alms to sustain himself, wandering from place to place until he reached his father’s capital city. His wife said to him, "This is the royal city. Alas, the suffering of hunger and cold is truly bitter! Once a prince, now a beggar! I wish for us to make this known and have the previous charge re-examined." Thereupon, they devised a plan to enter the king’s inner stables. In the final watch of the night, weeping as he faced the clear breeze, he sang out in a long, mournful wail, accompanying himself on the konghou (harp). From his high pavilion, the king heard the elegant singing, the lyrics of which were deeply resentful and sorrowful; wondering at it, he asked, "The sound of the singing to the konghou seems to be that of my son; for what reason has he come here?" He immediately asked the inner stables, "Who is singing and wailing?" They then brought the blind man before the king. Seeing the prince, the king asked with suppressed grief, "Who has harmed your body and brought this calamity upon you? My beloved son has lost his sight, yet I remained unaware; how then can I investigate the affairs of all the common people? O Heaven, O Heaven! How has my virtue declined!" The prince wept piteously and replied in apology, "It is truly because of my lack of filial piety that I have incurred the blame of Heaven. On a certain day of a certain month, I suddenly received your compassionate edict; having no way to voice my plea, I did not dare to evade my responsibility." The king, in his heart, knew that his new queen had acted wickedly, but without further investigation, he immediately imposed a severe punishment. At that time, in the Bodhi-tree (菩提樹) monastery, there was a great Arhat named Ghoṣa (瞿沙; Tang language: "Sublime Sound"), who possessed unobstructed mastery of the four analytical knowledges and was fully endowed with the three insights. The king brought his blind son to him, explained the situation, and prayed only for his compassion to restore the prince's sight. Having accepted the king's request, the Arhat immediately announced to the people of the country on that very day, "On a coming day, I wish to preach the sublime truth. Let each person bring a vessel and come here to listen to the Dharma, so as to collect your tears." Thereupon, people from near and far hastened to the site, and men and women gathered like clouds. At that time, the Arhat preached on the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination. Among all those who heard the Dharma, there was none who was not moved to deep sorrow, and they used the vessels they carried to collect their falling tears. When the preaching was finished, he collected all the tears and placed them in a golden basin, then made a vow, saying, "All that I have spoken is the ultimate truth of the Buddhas. If this truth is not genuine and my teaching contains errors, then so be it; but if it is not so, I wish to wash these blind eyes with the tears of the multitude, so that his sight may be restored and he may see as clearly as before." Having spoken these words, he took the tears and washed the eyes, and the eyes were immediately restored to sight. The king then rebuked his ministers and interrogated his officials; some were dismissed, some were banished, some were demoted, and some were put to death. The powerful and wealthy families were moved to the sandy desert to the northeast of the Snow Mountains.

issues: recurs from review_02-03: “I dare not forget my own unworthiness and wish to promote” → 敢忘庸鄙，紹隆法教: venturing to forget my own mediocrity, I wish to promote (Mizutani: 自らの凡庸なことも忘れて) | “The King of Himatala (呬摩呾羅國)” → the text has 呬摩呾羅王 (king, not 國) | fixed since the earlier review: 幽求名實; 苦其暑濕; 訖利多 now consistently Kṛta
en_revised: From here, traveling southeast, climbing mountains and traversing dangerous paths, crossing an iron bridge, and journeying more than one thousand li, one arrives at the country of Kaśmīra (迦濕彌羅國) (formerly called Jibin [罽賓], which is a corruption; it is in the territory of Northern India). The country of Kaśmīra is over seven thousand li in circumference. Its four borders are backed by mountains; the mountains are extremely steep and precipitous. Although there are gateways and paths, they are narrow and constricted, and since ancient times, neighboring enemies have been unable to attack or conquer it. The capital city of the country faces a great river to the west, measuring twelve or thirteen li from north to south and four or five li from east to west. It is suitable for agriculture, abounds in flowers and fruits, and produces dragon-breed horses, saffron (鬱金香), fire pearls, and medicinal herbs. The climate is cold and harsh, with much snow and little wind. The people wear woolen garments and white cotton (白㲲) clothing. The local customs are frivolous, and the people are mostly timid and cowardly. The country is protected by a dragon, and thus it has become powerful among its neighbors. The people are beautiful in appearance but deceitful in nature. They are fond of learning and are well-informed, believing in both heterodox and orthodox teachings. There are over one hundred saṃghārāmas and more than five thousand monks. There are four stūpas, all built by King Aśoka (無憂王), each containing over a pint of the Tathāgata’s relics. The *Country Records* (國志) state: "The land of this country was originally a dragon lake. In the past, when the Buddha, the World-Honored One, had subdued an evil spirit in the country of Uḍḍiyāna (烏仗那國) and wished to return to the Middle Kingdom, he rode through the air and, upon reaching the space above this country, said to Ānanda: 'After my parinirvāṇa, there will be an arhat named Madhyāntika (末田底迦) who will establish a kingdom in this land, settle the people, and propagate the Buddha-dharma.'" In the fiftieth year after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, the arhat Madhyāntika (末田底迦), a disciple of Ānanda, having attained the six supernatural powers and possessing the eight liberations, heard the Buddha’s prediction and felt great joy in his heart. He then came to this place, sat in meditation within the woods of the great mountain range (大山), and manifested great supernatural transformations. The dragon saw this and, having developed deep faith, asked what he desired. The arhat said, "I wish for you to grant me enough space within this lake to accommodate my knees." The dragon king thereupon caused the water to recede and offered the land to him. The arhat used his supernatural power to expand his body, and the dragon king exerted his strength to shrink the water; when the lake was empty and the water exhausted, the dragon turned and asked for the land back. The arhat left one pool for him in the northwest of this place, measuring one hundred and more li in circumference; the rest of his kin and dependents were to dwell in smaller pools separately. The dragon king said, "I have bestowed the entire lake and land upon you; I wish to provide offerings perpetually." Madhyāntika replied, "I shall soon enter parinirvāṇa without remainder; though I wish to accept your invitation, how would that be possible?" The dragon king requested again, "May five hundred arhats always receive my offerings until the Dharma comes to an end; after the Dharma has ended, I shall take back this country to serve as my dwelling pool." Madhyāntika acceded to his request. Once the arhat had obtained the land, he employed his great supernatural power to establish five hundred monasteries (伽藍). He purchased people of low status from various other countries to serve as laborers and provide for the monastic community. After Madhyāntika entered parinirvāṇa, those low-status people established their own leader. The neighboring countries despised their lowly caste and would not intermarry with them, calling them Kṛta (translated into Chinese as "bought"). At the present time, the spring water has already overflowed in many places. In the hundredth year after the Tathāgata’s nirvana, King Aśoka (無憂王) of the country of Magadha (摩揭陀國) ascended the throne and ruled the world; his majesty extended to distant lands. He had deep faith in the Three Jewels and cherished and nurtured the four types of living beings. At that time, there were five hundred arhat monks and five hundred ordinary monks, all of whom the king revered and supported without distinction. There was an ordinary monk named Mahādeva (摩訶提婆; translated into Chinese as "Great Heaven" [大天]), who was broad-minded and highly intelligent. He sought deeply into name and reality and composed a treatise through profound reflection that contradicted the holy teachings; those who heard of it followed his heterodox views. King Aśoka, unable to distinguish between the ordinary and the holy, sympathized with those he liked and sided with those close to him; he summoned the monks to the Ganges River (殑伽河), intending to drown them in the deep current and execute them all. When the arhats were faced with this mortal danger, they all exercised their supernatural powers, ascended into the void, and walked through the air, coming to this country to dwell in the mountains and hide in the valleys. When King Aśoka heard of this, he was afraid; he came in person to apologize and requested them to return to their own country. The arhats firmly refused to comply. King Aśoka built five hundred monasteries (伽藍) for the arhats and bestowed this entire country upon the community of monks. In the four-hundredth year after the Tathāgata’s nirvana, King Kaniṣka (迦膩色迦王) of the country of Gandhāra (健馱邏國) ascended the throne in accordance with the prophesied time; his royal influence spread far and wide, and people of diverse customs came to submit to his rule. In his leisure time from state affairs, he would study the Buddhist scriptures, daily inviting a monk to the palace to expound the Dharma. However, the various schools held divergent views, and the king was deeply perplexed, finding no way to resolve his doubts. At that time, the Venerable Pārśva (脇尊者) said: "Since the Tathāgata passed away, the years have grown distant; the disciples have formed different schools, and teachers have held divergent views, each relying on what they have heard and seen, and all contradicting one another." When the king heard this, he was deeply moved and grieved; after sighing in lamentation for a long while, he said to the Venerable: "By my humble remaining merit, I have followed in the footsteps of my predecessors; though far removed from the Sage, I am still fortunate. Venturing to forget my own unworthiness, I wish to promote and exalt the Dharma, explaining the Tripiṭaka in full according to the tenets of the various schools." The Venerable Pārśva said: "Your Majesty has planted roots of goodness in past lives and is richly endowed with blessings; that you should devote your mind to the Buddha-dharma is exactly what I desire." The king then issued a decree to near and far, summoning the sages and philosophers. Thereupon, they gathered from the four directions, traveling like stars across ten thousand miles; the brilliant and the wise all assembled. For seven days, he provided the four requisites as offerings. Wishing to hold a doctrinal discussion, he feared it would be noisy and chaotic. The king then expressed his thoughts to the monks, saying: "Those who have attained the fruits of sainthood may stay; those who are still bound by worldly fetters shall return." Even so, the number remained large. He issued another order: "Those who are 'without learning' (aśaikṣa) may stay; those who are 'still learning' (śaikṣa) shall return." Still, they were numerous. He issued yet another order: "Those who possess the three insights and are equipped with the six supernatural powers may stay; all others shall return." Yet, they were still numerous. He issued another order: "Those who have internally mastered the Three Baskets (Tripiṭaka) and externally attained the Five Sciences (pañcavidyā) may stay; all others shall return." Thereupon, four hundred and ninety-nine people were obtained. The king wished to hold the assembly in his own country, but he was troubled by its heat and humidity; he also wished to go to the stone cave in Rājagṛha where Mahākāśyapa had conducted the council. The Venerable Pārśva and the others deliberated, saying: "That is not possible. There are many non-Buddhists there, and their divergent views are tangled and confusing; one would be too busy responding to them to have any energy to compose the treatise. The hearts of the assembly are set on this country. This country is surrounded by solid mountains, guarded by yakṣas, its land is fertile, and its products are abundant; it is a place where sages and saints gather, and where spiritual immortals roam and dwell." The assembly deliberated on this, and all said: "This is appropriate." At that time, the king and the arhats arrived from there, established a monastery, and compiled the Tripiṭaka, intending to compose the *Vibhāṣā-śāstra*. At that time, the Venerable Vasumitra was outside the door mending his robes. The arhats said to Vasumitra: "Your fetters (kleśa) are not yet removed, and your pure deliberations are erroneous; you should go far away and not stay here." Vasumitra replied: "You worthies have no doubts regarding the Dharma; you act on behalf of the Buddha to transform others, and are now gathering the great meaning, wishing to compose a correct treatise. Although I am not clever, I have a rough understanding of the subtle words; I have also studied deeply the profound texts of the Tripiṭaka and the ultimate principles of the Five Sciences, and have grasped their essence." The arhats said: "Words cannot be like this. You should withdraw and dwell apart, quickly attain the state of 'no-learning' (aśaikṣa), and then join us; it will not be too late." Vasumitra said, "I regard the state of 'no-learning' (aśaikṣa) as I would spit or mucus; my aspiration is to seek the fruit of Buddhahood, not to pursue the lesser path. I shall throw this ball of thread, and before it falls to the ground, I shall certainly attain the holy fruit of 'no-learning'." At that time, the arhats rebuked him again, saying, "This is what is called a person of excessive pride. The fruit of 'no-learning' is praised by all Buddhas; you should attain it quickly to resolve the doubts of the assembly." Thereupon, Vasumitra threw the ball of thread. The devas in the air caught the ball of thread and pleaded, "You are about to realize the fruit of Buddhahood and will next succeed Maitreya (慈氏); as the most honored one in the three realms and the one upon whom all beings of the four births depend, why do you wish to realize the lesser fruit here?" When the arhats saw this event, they apologized for their fault, acknowledged his virtue, and invited him to be the chairperson; whenever there were doubts or discussions, they all took his decision as final. These five hundred sages first composed the *Upadeśa-śāstra* (鄔波第鑠論) (Original note: The old name, *Upadeśa-śāstra* (優波提舍論), is a corruption) in one hundred thousand stanzas, explaining the *Sūtra-piṭaka* (素呾纜藏) (Original note: The old name, *Sūtra-piṭaka* (修多羅藏), is a corruption). Next, they composed the *Vinaya-vibhāṣā-śāstra* (毘柰耶毘婆沙論) in one hundred thousand stanzas, explaining the *Vinaya-piṭaka* (毘奈耶藏) (Original note: The old name, *Vinaya-piṭaka* (毘那耶藏), is a corruption). Finally, they composed the *Abhidharma-vibhāṣā-śāstra* (阿毘達磨毘婆沙論) in one hundred thousand stanzas, explaining the *Abhidharma-piṭaka* (阿毘達磨藏) (Original note: Or it is called *Abhidharma-piṭaka* (阿毘曇藏), which is an abbreviation). In total, there are three hundred thousand stanzas and nine million six hundred thousand words, providing a complete explanation of the Tripiṭaka to be preserved for all eternity; they exhaustively explore every branch and detail, investigating both the shallow and the deep, so that the great principles are clarified once more, the subtle words are again revealed, and through their wide circulation, later students may rely upon them. King Kaniṣka (迦膩色迦王) then had the treatises incised on red copper plates, sealed them in stone cases, and erected a stūpa to store them inside. He commanded Yakṣa deities to guard the country, not allowing those of other schools to take these treatises out; those who wished to study them were to receive instruction within the country. When this work was completed, he returned his army to his capital. He went outside the western gate of this country, knelt facing east, and once again bestowed this entire country upon the community of monks. After King Kaniṣka passed away, the Kṛta (訖利多) tribe again claimed the kingship, expelled the monks, and destroyed the Buddha-dharma. The King of Himatala (呬摩呾羅王) (Original note: In the language of the Tang, "under the snow mountains") in the country of Tukhāra (覩貨邏國) was a descendant of the Śākya clan. Six hundred years after the Tathāgata’s nirvāṇa, he came to possess vast territories and inherited the royal enterprise; he planted his heart in the soil of the Buddha and poured his sentiments into the sea of the Dharma. Hearing that the Kṛta had destroyed the Buddha-dharma, he gathered three thousand brave warriors from his country, disguised them as merchants, and, carrying many precious goods while concealing weapons, entered this country. The king of this country treated them with special courtesy. From among the merchants, he further selected five hundred men who were fierce and resourceful; each hid a sharp blade in his sleeve and carried heavy treasures, personally bearing their offerings to present them to the king. At that moment, the King of Himatala (雪山下王) removed his cap and took the throne. The King of the Kṛta (訖利多王) was paralyzed with terror, whereupon the king beheaded him and commanded the subordinates, saying: "I am the King of Himatala in the country of Tukhāra (覩邏國). I am enraged by this base race’s public practice of tyrannical government, and therefore I have executed the guilty one today. As for all you common people, this is not your crime." However, he relocated the country’s ministers and officials to a foreign territory. Having pacified this country, he summoned the monks, established monasteries, and restored peace and order as before. Furthermore, outside the western gate of this country, he knelt facing east and offered alms to the assembly of monks. Because the Kṛta tribe had frequently caused the ruin of clans and the extinction of sacrifices on account of the monks, they had accumulated resentment for generations and detested the Buddha-dharma. As time passed, they again proclaimed themselves kings. Therefore, this country does not hold the faith in high esteem today, and they pay special attention to the temples of the non-Buddhist gods.

issues: recurs from review_02-03: “the great mountain (Pravaragiri)” → 至大山: a great mountain; no name in the Chinese
en_revised: Traveling over thirty li southeast from the small monastery, one reaches a great mountain, where there is an old monastery. Its design was once magnificent, but it is now largely overgrown and in ruins, with only a small multi-storied pavilion remaining in one corner. There are over thirty monks, all of whom study the Mahāyāna teachings. Formerly, the śāstra-master Saṃghabhadra (in the language of Tang, "Zhongxian" [Mass of the Virtuous]) composed the *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* (順正理論) here. In the various stūpas around the monastery, the relics of great arhats are preserved. Wild beasts and mountain apes gather flowers to offer them, never failing throughout the seasons, as if following a command. There are many miraculous traces in these mountains; for instance, stone walls are split horizontally, and horse tracks remain upon the peaks. All such phenomena, with their strange and unusual forms, are said to be the result of arhats and novices playing in groups, pointing and gesturing, or riding horses to and fro. Such remaining traces are too numerous to describe in detail.

issues: recurs from review_02-03: “Vikrītavana Monastery (商林伽藍)” → CBETA 商林 “Merchants’ Grove”; Vikrītavana rests on the emendation 買林 (Julien, Beal; Mizutani notes both)
en_revised: Traveling over two hundred li to the northwest of the royal city, one arrives at the Merchants’ Grove Monastery (商林伽藍; Vikrītavana if emended to 買林), where the śāstra master Pūrṇa (布剌拏; in the language of the Tang, "Complete") composed the *Exposition of the Vibhāṣā-śāstra* (*釋毘婆沙論*).
